abstract: Mitotic spindle positioning is essential for tissue architecture and organogenesis. In Drosophila neural stem cells, spindle positioning is attributed to apically enriched Dynein generating pulling forces on astral microtubules (MTs). Surprisingly, however, we find that the mitotic spindle consistently adopts a basal position along the apico-basal polarity axis, challenging the canonical model. We show that centrosomes at opposite spindle poles retain an intrinsic asymmetry in MT nucleation capacity inherited from their mother-daughter identity, with the apical daughter centrosome nucleating more MTs than the basal mother centrosome. Equalizing or reversing this asymmetry alters spindle positioning, demonstrating that basal spindle positioning critically depends on asymmetric centrosomal MT nucleation. Centrosome photoablation reveals that astral MTs generate pushing forces against the cell cortex that drive basal spindle positioning, whereas reducing apical Dynein-dependent pulling exacerbates basal spindle displacement, revealing an unexpected role for cortical pulling in limiting spindle displacement. Consistently, 3D Cytosim simulations incorporating cortical pulling forces together with MT nucleation-driven pushing forces, either asymmetric (wild-type or inverted) or symmetric, reproduce the observed spindle positioning. Together, our findings reveal that centrosome identity establishes an intrinsic asymmetry in MT nucleation that converts astral MT pushing into a dominant directional force for spindle positioning. This mechanism counteracts cortical pulling and contributes to daughter cell size asymmetry, uncovering an unexpected role for centrosome identity in determining where cells divide.
